issue: Must a defendant point to an actual state prosecution involving a substance not on the federal schedules before a state drug conviction can be disqualified as a predicate, or does a state statute that is facially broader than the federal schedules suffice?
provision: 18 U.S.C. § 924(e) (categorical approach to predicate offenses); Controlled Substances Act schedules, 21 U.S.C. § 802

sides.position: Actual-case requirement applies: a defendant must show a realistic probability, such as an actual state prosecution, that the state applies the statute to conduct outside the federal definition, even where the state statute is broader on its face
cases: United States v. Castillo-Rivera, 853 F.3d 218 (5th Cir. 2017) (en banc)
United States v. Augillard, No. 25-30192 (5th Cir. Aug. 18, 2026)

sides.position: No actual-case showing needed: when the state statute on its face reaches conduct beyond the federal definition, the statute's text itself makes the conviction broader and disqualifies it
cases: Salmoran v. Att'y Gen., 909 F.3d 73 (3d Cir. 2018)

this_court: adheres to the actual-case requirement (rejects the facial-mismatch rule)
quote: Our “actual case” requirement not only places us on the short side of a 10-1 circuit split, but, more importantly, puts our circuit’s precedent in tension with the Supreme Court’s.
cite: United States v. Augillard, No. 25-30192 (5th Cir. 2026)
